title: Security & Export Playbook: Admin Activity Retention and Offsite Export (Kestrel Health Systems)
summary: High-level security review focused on admin telemetry: Kestrel needs granular admin event capture, multi-destination export (on-prem syslog + cloud S3), 7+ years retention for investigation-ready records, and KMS key control. Redwood outlined current capture surface, export patterns, retention tiers, and suggested pilot steps (test export to dev S3 + on-prem syslog sink).
next_steps: Jordan: Share SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 artifacts + architecture diagram by 2026-12-18
Priya: Provision a 2-week test export config for Kestrel dev account (S3 + syslog) by 2026-12-22
Marko: Provide sample retention policy and legal required retention ranges by 2026-12-17
action_items: Jordan - Send SOC2 Type II report link and redacted audit summary (due 2026-12-18)
Priya - Create export config yaml and test run, include sample kafka connector logs (due 2026-12-22)
Marko - Confirm whether audit evidence must be WORM/immutable for 7 years (due 2026-12-17)
Sara - Review proposed export contract language around PII egress and provide redlines (due 2026-12-21)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/time: 2026-12-15 16:00 PST
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Dr. Emily Rivera (CISO - Kestrel), Marko Novak (Platform Eng), Sara Liu (Legal)

[00:00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for taking the time, i'll kick us off. We're here to cover admin activity capture, what we log, export options, and retention because i know Kestrel has some long-term e-discovery and evidentiary requirements.
[00:00:12] Dr. Rivera: Yep, thanks Jordan. We have some auditors next Q and also internal privacy regs — we need to know exactly what you capture and whether we can export it to our lake or to on-prem SIEM.
[00:00:22] Priya: Great. Quick outline: we'll run through the event taxonomy, show how exports work (S3, syslog, Kafka, direct push), retention tiers, and KMS options for key control and rotation. Please stop me any time.
[00:00:35] Marko: real quick — our constraints: data residency in US-EAST, keys must be customer-managed for prod, and anything with admin context kept for min 7 years in immutable storage.
[00:00:47] Jordan: understoood. Priya, can you walk through what we capture under "admin events"?
[00:00:52] Priya: Sure. At a high level we capture: user and service principal authentication attempts (success/fail), console UI actions for admin pages, API calls that modify config (create/delete/model-deployments/role changes), route and policy changes, RBAC grant/revoke, SSO provisioning events, user session metadata (IP, user agent), and data-access-evidence (who invoked model, input/output hashes when requested). We also capture system-generated events like autoscaler decisions and deployment rollbacks but those are labeled as infra events.
[00:01:25] Dr. Rivera: you said input/output hashes — can you clarify?
[00:01:28] Priya: yes — by default we don't log raw prompts or plaintext model outputs to the admin audit stream. For traceability we can store a SHA256 hash of payloads (or redacted snippets) and a short metadata blob with token counts, model id, and request id. That allows determinism in investigations without keeping full content by default. If a customer requests full payload capture, we have an opt-in per-tenant toggle and that gets flagged in policy and in the retention rules — usually only allowed under contract.
[00:02:00] Marko: That hash approach is fine, just need to ensure we can do reproducible matches if legal asks. Also want to confirm KMS routing: can keys be in our AWS account?
[00:02:10] Priya: Yes. For Private and Dedicated customers we support customer-managed keys (CMKs) in your AWS account. There's a KMS handshake where Redwood only gets envelopes encrypted with your public key; Redwood never holds the plaintext key. Key rotation is supported — rotation events are logged and the audit stream includes key identifiers and rotation timestamps.
[00:02:36] Sara: for legal we need chain-of-custody metadata — i.e., who exported what, when, and to which destination. Is that present in the audit bundle?
[00:02:44] Priya: Absolutely. Every export produces a manifest: export id, export initiator (user/service), destination uri, object checksums, and a signed timestamp. We can optionally sign manifests with a Redwood signing key and also include customer-provided signatures if you prefer.
[00:03:02] Dr. Rivera: talk to me about export destinations — we want to push to both our on-prem syslog collector and S3 in a locked bucket.
[00:03:09] Priya: We support multiple sinks concurrently. Options: 
- S3 (per-tenant path; supports SSE-KMS and customer CMK)
- Syslog/TCP (TLS) to your on-prem SIEM collector
- Kafka or Kinesis streams for streaming ingest
- Direct SFTP with signed objects
You can configure synchronous or asynchronous delivery; for high assured delivery to on-prem we recommend syslog over TLS with local buffering and a retry backoff.
[00:03:46] Marko: buffering — if we lose connectivity do you keep events for re-delivery?
[00:03:50] Priya: yes, the export agent buffers locally in the Redwood control plane for up to X days (configurable per contract) and will retry. For Dedicated/private deployments you can also deploy an operator to capture and forward events directly from within your VPC so you control disk retention. There's also a nearline archival tier that offloads to our long-term store encrypted with your CMK until you pull.
[00:04:12] Dr. Rivera: retention tiers — can we do 7 years immutable plus a hot 90-day window?
[00:04:18] Priya: Typical pattern is: hot window (90-180 days) for quick investigations with normal read access; cold/nearline for 1-3 years; and long-term WORM/immutable retention for 7+ years in archival storage. The long-term tier is handled via export to your S3 with a bucket lock policy or object lock enabled, or via our export manifest that you ingest and then write to your immutable store. Redwood can also write directly to an S3 bucket in your account with object lock enabled.
[00:04:45] Sara: any restrictions on object-lock when using CMK?
[00:04:48] Priya: No direct restrictions — but object lock settings are enforced at the bucket level in your account. We will write objects with the metadata and can set retention headers, but the bucket configuration must allow it. We'll provide the deployment playbook for the required IAM roles.
[00:05:05] Jordan: quick pause — any SOC2/ISO artifacts i should surface now?
[00:05:09] Priya: I have checklist notes. Jordan will share the full SOC2 Type II and our ISO27001 scope bundle after the call.
[00:05:17] Jordan: yes i'll share.
[00:05:20] Dr. Rivera: logging fidelity — are there gaps? i.e., do you capture full request/response latencies per API call and do you preserve caller identity when services act on behalf of users?
[00:05:30] Priya: We capture request/response metadata including latency, status codes, request id, and caller identity (user or service token). For service-to-service actions we include a delegated-by field if available. Sometimes the delegated field is null if external systems don't propagate identity; we recommend instrumenting upstream to attach federated identity for full traceability.
[00:05:53] Marko: curious about cost — storing 7 years of admin telemetry sounds expensive. what's the typical unit cost?
[00:05:58] Jordan: cost varies by retention tier and export destination. Redwood charges for outbound export egress and optional long-term storage; if data lands in your S3 you pay storage in your account. Our optimize team can model expected volume based on your request rates and provide a compression/aggregation strategy (e.g., log compaction and batching) to reduce bytes stored.
[00:06:20] Dr. Rivera: encryption in transit — syslog is TLS but do you support mTLS?
[00:06:24] Priya: We support TLS mutual auth for syslog and can accept client certs from your collectors. For streaming via Kafka, we support SASL/SSL and client certificates. S3 uploads use https and can be authenticated with presigned post or direct PutObject with IAM role.
[00:06:41] Sara: on the legal front we need export controls — specifically that Redwood won't inspect exported payloads unless explicitly contracted. Is that included?
[00:06:48] Jordan: yes standard clause — outbound exports to customer destinations are considered customer-owned; Redwood retains minimal metadata for delivery proof and troubleshooting and access is logged. We'll include explicit language in the export addendum.
[00:06:59] Dr. Rivera: what about RBAC events? Can we see role grant history and who approved it?
[00:07:05] Priya: Yes, we capture grant/revoke events, role definitions at the time of grant (a snapshot), approver id if approval workflow used, and timestamps. If you use SSO provisioning events we record SCIM changes and the original SAML assertion id if present.
[00:07:22] Marko: any quick demo of the manifest or a sample export file?
[00:07:26] Priya: I've got a short snippet, i'll paste the sample manifest link in the chat after. Sample manifest includes: export_id, start_time, end_time, checksum_list, object_locations, initiator, signed_by.
[00:07:39] Dr. Rivera: perfect. Another question: are admin audit logs tamper-evident inside Redwood before export?
[00:07:45] Priya: Logs inside our system are append-only with integrity checksums and we maintain a write-once stream internally. For extra assurance we can publish periodic signed checkpoints (hash chain roots) to your account or to a public ledger if needed. This makes tamper detection easier.
[00:08:02] Sara: chain of custody plus signed checkpoints would satisfy our counsel for many cases. We'll want to document the verification steps in the evidence pack.
[00:08:10] Jordan: noted. we'll add that to the playbook.
[00:08:14] Dr. Rivera: testing and pilot — Marko, what's your preferred path?
[00:08:18] Marko: we want a low-friction pilot — start with dev account export to our S3 dev bucket (encrypted with our CMK) plus a syslog sink to our staging SIEM. We'll validate manifests and checksum verification. If all good, we'll move to prod and enable object lock.
[00:08:35] Priya: timeline wise i can spin up the export config for dev and run a 2-week capture, include the manifest signing, and show replay/re-delivery. That will exercise buffering and retry.
[00:08:47] Dr. Rivera: perfect. Sara, anything from legal about content?
[00:08:50] Sara: we need to review the addendum. Particularly the clause about Redwood's temporary caching for retrying exports — we want assurances around deletion after redelivery and retention limits for that buffer. Also indemnity language around exported PII.
[00:09:05] Jordan: understood — we'll propose specific retention bounds for control-plane buffers and include it in the export contract language.
[00:09:12] Priya: also to note, for Dedicated or Private deployment models we can deploy a local operator that never transmits pre-processed events to Redwood; in that topology the buffering and replay are entirely under your control which helps legal.
[00:09:26] Marko: that topology may be preferred if we need absolute control. Can you send a diagram for the operator flow?
[00:09:31] Priya: yes, i'll include that in the playbook.
[00:09:35] Dr. Rivera: any limitations on retention metadata size? for instance we store extended attributes for certain events — would that make objects large?
[00:09:43] Priya: object size is configurable but we typically cap per-event stored metadata to avoid runaway costs. For extended attributes we recommend storing them in your downstream store and reference them via keys in the manifest; we can include pointers.
[00:09:58] Jordan: closing loop — recap next steps and owners?
[00:10:02] Jordan: Jordan will share SOC2/ISO docs; Priya builds dev export for 2-week pilot; Marko provides retention constraints and confirms WORM requirements; Sara returns redlines for export addendum.
[00:10:17] Dr. Rivera: thanks all.
[00:10:19] Priya: i'll drop the sample manifest and a quick playbook link in the calendar invite follow-up.

[00:10:30] --- Freeform transcript continues with captured Q&A, interruptions, and side notes. ---
[00:10:30] Speaker 1: so let me ask about the timeline for export verification steps, do you have recommended checks?
[00:10:36] Priya: yes: checksum verification, manifest signature validation, object count vs expected, and replayed event integrity. We also recommend running weekly digest queries for the hot window to detect unusual admin churn.
[00:10:52] Speaker 2: (background noise) sorry one sec, i'll mute —
[00:10:56] Jordan: no problem.
[00:11:10] Priya: a couple of real-world notes — one customer stored 7 years of manifests in compressed archives and used a small bloom-filter index to find relevant exports for legal holds. It cut search time and cost.
[00:11:25] Marko: nice. Do you provide an index?
[00:11:28] Priya: We can provide index files as part of the manifest package. The index contains event type, time range, and a quick hash map for hits.
[00:11:37] Dr. Rivera: about SSO: we use Okta — will SAML assertion IDs map into your logs?
[00:11:43] Priya: yes, we ingest SAML assertion IDs and SCIM change logs if Okta is configured with provisioning hooks. That gives you a direct link from an auth event to the SCIM change.
[00:11:52] Sara: any international export restrictions? we operate solely in the US but might have global staff.
[00:11:57] Priya: exports can be region-restricted; we can enforce that audit objects never leave your selected region and we can set geo-fencing on exports. For cross-border staff we log the origin IP but sensitive content stays within the specified region unless you opt-in.
[00:12:12] Jordan: okay wrapping up — i'll send the artifacts and schedule the pilot kickoff for 2026-12-22. Thanks everyone.
[00:12:21] Dr. Rivera: thanks.
[00:12:23] Meeting end.
